entries.title: Trump's Economy Speech Veers Into an Extended Riff on Communism
entries.summary: The president dedicated several minutes of his Las Vegas speech to denouncing Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed and Wisconsin’s Francesca Hong.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump came to Las Vegas on Wednesday to rally voters on the economy and tax relief. But, after a pivotal week for left-leaning candidates in Michigan and Wisconsin, he couldn’t help but turn to communism.

“You lose your home, you lose your apartment, and that’s where the communists will take us,” Trump said. “You got to nip it in the bud.”

The president’s broadsides at the Red Rocks Casino came during a nearly 75-minute rally, evoking repeated cheers from the audience. Trump diverged from his economic remarks multiple times, including minutes-long segments calling out this week’s main characters: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who edged out moderate Rep. Haley Stevens by a narrow margin, and Wisconsin gubernatorial hopeful Francesca Hong, who went viral over old posts describing a hatred of Thanksgiving (and Christmas, and Halloween).

El-Sayed’s primary win was the latest example of left-wing challengers succeeding against more moderate, establishment-backed Democrats. It’s a shift that has coincided with a deepening party splinter since Trump entered office — and one Republicans hope to take advantage of during the summer campaign season by amplifying distrust of communism to push more centrist voters away from progressive candidates.

El-Sayed’s victory makes that effort easier, Trump said Wednesday.

“The polls say we do better against the communists,” the president said. “So he won, and so I think I’m happy.”

Trump has been attacking communism for some time, but he gained fresh ammunition this week after more of Hong’s past commentary — including wanting to abolish Thanksgiving and voicing disdain for other holidays — circulated ahead of the state’s Aug. 11 primary.

A member of the Wisconsin General Assembly and the Democratic Socialists of America, Hong has also been criticized for past calls to abolish the police, among other left-wing positions. But her Turkey Day opinion — which Hong has since walked back, telling Politico on Wednesday that it’s actually her favorite holiday — was a welcome talking point and easy target for Republicans. Wisconsin Rep. Tom Tiffany’s campaign even reposted comments from Hong’s own press team.

Trump blasted her on Wednesday as he called communism “the greatest threat to our country,” including both World Wars, Pearl Harbor and 9/11.

“And in Wisconsin, the communists have a woman who said that the holiday of Thanksgiving should be immediately abolished, and the police — the police only exist to, quote, ‘uphold white supremacy,’” Trump said, calling Hong a “lunatic.” “We can’t let them get into office.”

Republicans have a lower opinion of socialism than Democrats, who are the only partisan group to view the ideology more positively than capitalism, a 2025 Gallup poll found. Those dynamics have been present in Michigan and Wisconsin’s primaries this month: Multiple polls show Hong with a dominant lead in the primary race, and surveys conducted prior to the Thanksgiving comments’ resurfacing showed her virtually tied with Tiffany for the general election. And El-Sayed will face Republican Mike Rogers, who posted a video calling his opponent a “radical leftist” on Wednesday.

“But everyone, every time this has happened ... you go through squalor. And add the word again: filth, crime, death, destruction, embarrassment,” Trump said. “When I watch Abdul — he’s full of shit.”
entries.author: Ben T.N. Mause

entries.title: Trump Is Losing the Battle With Public Opinion on Data Centers
entries.summary: His administration’s efforts to speed up data center construction is stoking the very backlash that could stymie growth.
entries.content:
The residents of Boulder City, Nevada, are raging mad at the federal government.

The Trump administration unilaterally approved a data center on a tract of public land within the city’s jurisdiction this summer without giving residents a say in the matter and without conducting an environmental assessment specific to the project.

“Tyranny,” one resident described it in front of the City Council in July.

“I would call it a surprise attack,” said another.

The Boulder City project is part of the Trump administration’s efforts to make the country the “number one superpower in artificial intelligence,” as dictated by President Donald Trump’s slate of executive orders intended to pave the way for quicker data center development and support the AI industry.

Those federal efforts have amounted to opening a handful of public and federal lands to construction, and waiving public review periods and environmental guardrails — changes industry watchers say don’t necessarily address the biggest hurdles to faster development.

What they have done is further fuel one of the few forces powerful enough to actually block the momentum of the AI industry: local anxiety.

Or, in the case of Boulder City, rage.

“We do not have guardrails for artificial intelligence. We do not have Congress implementing rules to try to navigate what happens when these corporations succeed because we have become a nation that is pay-to-play,” Gabriel Cornejo, a Democrat who ran an unsuccessful campaign for Nevada’s 1st Congressional District, said at the City Council meeting. “That concentration of power is going to yield, unfortunately, the pitchforks.”
Climate Colorado River Boulder City, NV AP-26212493447862 (8640x5760, AR: 1.50)In recent months, the public has swung 49 percentage points against data centers, according to Heatmap polling from Embold Research. Skepticism of data centers is bipartisan, and doesn’t fall neatly along lines of age or geography.

Rep. Dina Titus (D-Nevada) said she’d been hearing more from Nevada residents about data centers since the Boulder City project was approved.

The Trump administration’s efforts to speed up development have exacerbated local fears around AI infrastructure, she said, especially as so many massive facilities pop up around the country.

“They don’t like data centers, period,” Titus said. “But they certainly don’t like having the choice taken away from them.”

Last year, Trump laid out a sweeping plan to accelerate data center infrastructure. He called for reducing environmental regulations, recommended making federal lands available for construction and directed federal agencies to get rid of rules that hindered the AI industry.

That’s what his administration has done. The Department of Energy and Department of Defense have started partnering with companies to build at federal sites. Earlier this year, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers allowed for data centers developers in need of Clean Water Act permits to skip the public notice period.

The Environmental Protection Agency has proposed allowing data centers to begin construction before facilities receive air permits and eliminating public participation requirements for another environmental permit.

Even the Department of Justice has gotten involved, intervening in a Clean Air Act lawsuit between the NAACP and Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI. Justice officials argue that they have the power to dismiss the case entirely, saying the NAACP’s lawsuit threatens federal policy interests and the “immediate and pressing” need to expand energy infrastructure.

But negotiations over permitting reform in Congress, which has much of the authority to fundamentally reshape the laborious permitting process, have been stuck for years in partisan gridlock. Those talks have become only marginally more fruitful this session. Trump’s interference with clean energy projects and moves weakening environmental protections have threatened possible compromise.

And despite Trump’s best efforts to remove challenges for data centers, building them hasn’t gotten much easier in the last year, industry experts said. Many of the aspects that make building AI infrastructure difficult simply aren’t in the administration’s control.

Local zoning, state and municipal permits, electric grid interconnection and supply chain issues all tend to be more significant constraints than federal permitting, said Ben Schifman, a senior technology fellow at the Institute for Progress.

Under the direction of the Energy Department, federal regulators have stepped in to try to speed up the interconnection process, which can delay projects up to six or seven years. But ultimately, that will require regional grid operators to reform their rules governing how data centers connect to the grid.

“My sense is that there has not been a major change, if any change at all, to the overall permitting landscape for data centers,” Schifman said.

Data centers have broken new computing capacity records every seven months since late 2024, doubling the amount each time — consistent with the boom in construction after OpenAI’s GPT-4 model was released, said Ben Cottier, a senior researcher at Epoch AI.

“It’s possible that without these executive orders, it would have slowed down, but it hasn’t slowed down,” Cottier said. “In terms of our observations of the data, there isn’t a clear acceleration or anything.”

What has accelerated is public opposition to projects, often over the same issues the Trump administration is trying to ease oversight around: water quality, air quality and speed.

“People don’t trust Trump on environmental issues, period,” said Darrell West, a senior fellow with the Brookings Institution.
Lee Zeldin AP-26141584005217 (8640x5760, AR: 1.50)West attributes the backlash over projects across the country in part to distrust over the president’s frequent meetings with Silicon Valley billionaires.

Without local support, projects falter. A data center project challenged by local opposition has roughly a 50% chance of being canceled.

“The Trump administration has failed in really accelerating federal permitting because most of the permits required to build a data center are at the local level,” West said. “And over the last six months, community opposition has accelerated. That has slowed down approvals.”

Even state leaders who back Trump have started to balk at the speed with which data centers are being developed. Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas announced a data center moratorium until state regulators could conduct comprehensive audits of all projects — including data on water consumption and power usage.

People in towns where data centers developers are looking to build have described “reckless” processes and feeling steamrolled.

The Trump administration has, on occasion, acknowledged this pushback as a hurdle. Energy Secretary Chris Wright has noted the anger in rural communities over big projects, but has called concerns about the facilities “overblown.”

“The development of data centers can be almost anywhere,” Wright said in a press briefing during an AI event hosted by his agency. “The challenge has been which communities should host them.”

To counter souring public sentiments, Trump has begun waging a public relations campaign on the behalf of data centers.

At an event announcing additions to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, invitees included a school superintendent from Richland Parish, Louisiana, and a teacher in his district, who credited Meta’s data center with $50,000 bonuses for educators in the area.

“This isn’t all negative stuff,” Trump said at the event. “You have communities that really want the data centers, and frankly, those are the smart communities because it means tremendous numbers of jobs, very little actual disruption.”

Ultimately, he issued a directive: “You can’t fight it,” he said. “You have to go with it.”

But polling suggests that communities willing to go along with data centers have become fewer and further between since the administration has started pushing for quicker development.

The administration and developers are in alignment on wanting it to be easier to build data centers. But speeding up permitting doesn’t address the main hurdle for builders, Staci Pies, senior vice president of government affairs and policy at INCOMPAS, said.

“What requires more time is being very responsive to the community, and understanding what local benefits the community needs and wants, and striking that bargain,” she said.

People in Boulder City have been more outspoken in their opposition to data centers than they were before federal officials stepped in, said Lisa LaPlante, the city’s communications manager.

“There’s a lot of questions that are now being raised that weren’t being raised before,” LaPlante said.

The city was still working on its approach to AI infrastructure developments when the Bureau of Land Management approved the data center project without any local input.

And even though the site is on public lands, Boulder City will be required to provide emergency services and some utilities. So local officials are gearing up to make their own policies that will govern data center development. In a way, they’re being forced to create those rules, LaPlante said.

In a unanimous decision, the City Council decided to appeal the Bureau of Land Management approval.

A bit over a week later, Rep. Titus sent a letter to Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo, asking him to halt state tax abatements for data centers on federal lands until state lawmakers review the issue.

“It feels like we’re the test for all of this, to see what happens when a data center is basically forced on a city,” LaPlante said.
entries.author: Mara Hoplamazian

entries.title: Talk to Tom: Restaurant Recs for D.C., Maryland ... and Germany!
entries.summary: Plus, ways to help the restaurant industry, and why tuna crudo is on every menu.
entries.content:
Welcome to Talk to Tom, the dining advice column that aims to point you toward good meals, steer you from the dross and solve your pressing restaurant queries. Look for a fresh Q&A every Thursday in this space.

Questions and comments can be submitted to TalkToTom@notus.com. Submissions may be edited for length and clarity.

I don't have a ton of money, but I'd like to support the industry. What’s the best way to back those restaurants we love besides just dining there?

Every restaurant operator I reached out to appreciated your question. These are tough times for the industry; even small gestures of appreciation help.

“Restaurants need and love praise from guests,” says Amy Brandwein, the chef of Centrolina and Piccolina in CityCenter. “So share your love with news outlets, social media and review [sites]. That is a way to generate more business without spending a dime.”

Word of mouth is crucial, says Anthony Jones, the chef at Marcus DC in NoMa, who makes a habit of frequenting area mom-and-pops, even if it’s just an ice cream shop.

If you have some money to spare, restaurateurs say buying gift cards is a boon to a business. “It’s an immediate injection of revenue for us and a promise of future business,” says Bill Jensen, the vision behind Reveler’s Hour in Adams Morgan. Patrice Cleary of Purple Patch and Joia Burger in Mount Pleasant likes the idea of purchasing, say, four $25 gift certificates and passing them out to a kids program or other charity. Who knows, she says; “You may introduce somebody else to a [new] restaurant.”

Remember that not every meal away from home has to be extravagant, says Matt Adler, the chef behind Caruso’s Grocery and Cucina Morini in the Capitol Hill East and Mount Vernon Square neighborhoods, respectively. “Even just grabbing a bowl of pasta and a glass of wine at the bar on a slower night makes a big difference for a restaurant,” he says, “especially during slower restaurant months.” Jones suggests forming a group or club to try a wider variety of dishes and spread out the cost of a meal.

Since moving to Montgomery County 15 years ago, I’ve encountered few really good restaurants. Can you recommend anything, aside from strictly sushi spots, with price less of a concern than quality? (I’m really glad you’re doing this here, along with many other of my favorite writers from The Washington Post.)

Thanks for the question and the welcome.

When I think about Maryland’s most populous county — with more than a million people spread over about 500 square miles — the restaurants I never tire of visiting suggest a U.N. buffet.
DC0A7865 copyb.jpg (8855x6566, AR: 1.35)My tried-and-true spots are:

  • The Salt Line for pleasing seafood, including an ace lobster roll, in Bethesda.
  • Melina for polished Greek in North Bethesda.
  • Beteseb for Ethiopian in Silver Spring, where my current fascination is dullet, or boiled, ground beef tripe spiked with jalapeño, mitmita and cardamom.
  • Cielo Rojo for Mexican in Takoma Park, a fetching retreat that has me scraping the bottom of my brick-red bowl of pozole, thick with chicken and thrumming with dried chiles.
  • Chennai Hoppers and Peter Chang for admirable Indian and Chinese, respectively, in Gaithersburg.
Different as the restaurants are, they share consistency, comfort and choiceness.

My biggest (pettiest) restaurant pet peeve is the ubiquity of tuna crudo. It's a delicious dish, but everyone has it and I'm ready to move on!

Any day now, I expect Olive Garden to start selling the Italian appetizer — simply dressed raw fish, typically splashed with olive oil, salt and citrus — which I agree is seemingly everywhere these days.

Behind the “Odyssey”-esque ubiquity swim several forces: a raw fish boom led long ago by sushi, the ongoing popularity of Italian coastal cuisine, the wide availability of sushi-grade tuna and the ease of preparation. Compared to a cooked dish, crudo involves minimal labor and saves on waste.

Finally, tuna crudo gives even a mainstream menu a whiff of cachet.

Tom, my last trip to Germany was when the country name started with “West.” My husband and I are nonetheless heading to Frankfurt for a week in early September with friends who recently moved there from Baltimore, and we would love your recommendations for restaurants. Cost doesn’t matter; value does. One person doesn’t eat red meat and another doesn’t eat seafood/shellfish. Ideally, at least one option would serve spaetzle and schnitzel.

Some of the innovative places that should land on your list are Emma Metzler, set inside the Museum of Applied Arts and popular for its house-baked bread, nose-to-tail cooking and a terrace overlooking a park; Chairs, where the regionally focused menu changes monthly and the wines are natural; Rausch, which serves a tasting menu featuring modern German fare (and where I’m told Friday lunch is the prime time to go); and Main Tower Restaurant & Lounge, whose menu combines Asian and Austrian influences and whose dining room sits high in the sky in the banking district.

For more traditional German cooking, one option is the lively, cash-only Ebbelwoi Unser, dressed with communal tables and home to Hessian classics like schnitzel with green sauce and fresh apple wine.

Help! I need a “nice-ish” D.C. restaurant that can accommodate a range of appetites and won’t cost a fortune. (I’m paying.) 

You want Unconventional Diner, the spirited American restaurant near the convention center (get it?) that never fails to please. No issue if one of you wants meat, one wants plants, another diner hopes for something adventurous. Chef-owner David Deshaies offers something for everyone on his menu: a meatloaf fueled with Sriracha for heat and Gruyere cheese for succulence; a refreshing and beautiful Thai salad; crackling duck confit with steaming bao buns in a circle of accessories. (The idea with the last dish is to create your own duck sandwiches with cilantro, hoisin sauce, chiles and more.)

Your question prompted a reunion with the restaurant over the weekend, when it was packed with Otakon attendees, many dressed as their favorite characters from Japanese video games and comics. A companion and I split a heaping helping of “nachos” coaxed from kale and striped with electric sauces, and a stellar chicken parm escorted with a bundle of spaghetti tossed in butter, Parmesan and chicken stock for added flavor. Busy as the place was, the staff took time to charm. As I debated between miso salmon and that duck confit, a server asked, “What’s your aim tonight?” before describing each dish in detail.

All this, at a price that will make you as happy as the food: The generous entrees — buttermilk pancakes for dinner, if you’re so inclined! — average an agreeable $24.

Direct me to your preferred banh mi in the DMV, please. 

If forced to eat one sandwich for the rest of my life — and with apologies to France’s jambon-buerre, the Middle East’s shawarma and New Orleans’ muffuletta — I’d cast my fate with the Vietnamese wonder built with a crisp baguette and a combination of meat, tangy vegetables and a spread of butter or mayonnaise. And I’d eat them all at Bánh Mì Oi in Falls Church. (“Oi” is a call to attention in Vietnamese, similar to “hey.”)

The signature banh mi packs ham, pâté, pork bologna and pork belly along with traditional enhancers of cucumber, cilantro, pickled carrots, daikon and aioli between slices of a roll that’s at once airy, crisp and fluffy. The monster bread, baked on site, is so good, people ask to buy just the base; requests are limited to five rolls per order, says owner Yeanie Bach, citing the business’s small kitchen. Other fillings include a delectable warm tofu seasoned with star anise, and Nashville (truly) hot chicken.

Know before going in that there are fewer than 40 small stools spread across two small floors and outside. Expect a line. Know, too, Bánh Mì Oi delivers.

Clearly, I’m not the only fanboy. Bach says she sells an average of 1,200 to 1,500 of her hits — per day.
entries.author: Tom Sietsema

entries.title: Is The Epstein Investigation Almost Over? Depends On Who You Ask.
entries.summary: Oversight Chair James Comer told NOTUS he expects new activity at the Justice Department as a result of his probe.
entries.content:
Republicans and Democrats on the House Oversight Committee say they want the same thing: justice for the victims of the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

But whether the committee’s investigation is wrapping up or just starting will depend entirely on the November election.

Republicans leading the investigation now are finishing interviews and a report as the midterm elections near, hoping to prompt the Justice Department to investigate individuals from the network surrounding Epstein. Democrats, who think they’ll control the panel in January, say there’s a lot more to mine before the probe is over.

Republicans, led by Oversight Committee Chair James Comer (R-Kentucky), are finalizing plans to wrap up their Epstein investigation as the midterm elections near, with Comer indicating that the committee will probably make criminal referrals in the case. Top Justice Department officials signaled earlier this year there would be no more prosecutions after a review of millions of files related to Epstein.

“The Department of Justice said the case was closed when we started it,” Comer told NOTUS about the probe into the network surrounding Epstein.

He predicted a report and criminal referrals from his panel will force new action from the Justice Department, even if that work continues after his tenure.

“I’m going to go out on a limb and say the case will be reopened when we’re done.”

Comer, who is term-limited in his position at the top of the committee even if Republicans keep the House, has hauled a list of 19 high-profile witnesses in for closed-door interviews. Some witnesses including former President Bill Clinton and Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates told the committee they barely knew Epstein and had no knowledge of his crimes. Others, such as billionaire Leon Black, detailed a closer relationship with Epstein but issued the same denials about any illegal activity related to sexual misconduct.

Among the witnesses are people with deep ties to Republican and Democratic figures. The group includes billionaire Les Wexner, a longtime Democratic donor; former Trump Attorney General Bill Barr; former Obama White House Counsel Kathy Ruemmler; and former Trump Labor Secretary Alex Acosta.

Black, who has donated significantly to both parties, drew intense scrutiny from investigators in the past few months. The private equity billionaire told investigators he paid Epstein over $150 million for tax and estate planning between 2012 and 2017. That was after Epstein pleaded guilty in 2008 in Florida to soliciting prostitution from a minor. Comer issued subpoenas after Black declined to answer some of the panel's key questions during a voluntary interview in June: one subpoena for a deposition, and another for nondisclosure agreements that lawmakers maintain are between Black and women who may have been associated with Epstein. Black has turned over one NDA to investigators, a source familiar with the matter said.

Investigators say they’re looking into whether any witnesses lied during their testimony.

According to Comer, victims have said some of the people deposed have made untrue statements. “We’re doing everything in our ability, and we’re going to continue to work with the victims,” Comer said.

Democrats have criticized Republicans’ handling of the Epstein probe, pointing out that witnesses were not required to testify under oath and that Comer did not publicly release recordings of most of the interviews (save for Bill and Hillary Clinton).

California Rep. Robert Garcia, currently the top Democrat on the oversight panel, is in line to take over if his party wins the House and says the investigation has a lot more ground to cover.

“There’s no question that the investigation will continue into the next couple of years,” Garcia told NOTUS. “The fact that the chairman has been unwilling to put most of the interviews under oath is really problematic, and there’s a lot of folks who are still going to have more information.”

But Randall Eliason, a former assistant U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, told NOTUS that the fight over whether to swear in witnesses is mostly about “atmospherics” and that “legally, it doesn’t matter.”

“Whether or not you are under oath, lying to Congress during an investigation is a crime,” Eliason said. “It certainly wouldn’t prevent someone from bringing criminal charges if they thought the elements were there.”

Despite their criticisms of Comer’s probe, Democrats told NOTUS they would support criminal referrals stemming from the investigation.

“I’d want to wait and see who exactly Chairman Comer is considering, but we would be supportive of going after folks,” Garcia told NOTUS. “We think there’s enough evidence for the Justice Department to take stronger action.”

California Rep. Ro Khanna, another Democrat on the panel who teamed up with Kentucky GOP Rep. Thomas Massie to force the release of the files, told NOTUS he supports criminal referrals.

“We need a call to remove people with serious allegations from their positions on important corporations or boards, or having their names on important buildings,” Khanna said. “And we need a clear call for the release of the rest of the files.”

The Justice Department released about 3.5 million pages of documents related to the Epstein investigation after a veto-proof majority of Congress passed a bill forcing the federal government to publicly turn them over. Batches of the files were released late last year, featuring heavy redactions and the accidental release of sensitive information related to victims. The Justice Department withheld more than 2 million pages, citing the privacy of victims, privileged information and other legally protected content.

Comer is still planning to bring in several additional witnesses before concluding the investigation this fall. Black is scheduled to return for another interview with the committee on Sept. 3. Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, who could be confirmed by the Senate to permanently take the top post at Justice soon, is supposed to speak with the panel after that process concludes. Blanche, who at the time was the no. 2 official at the DOJ, oversaw the release of the Epstein files, according to former Attorney General Pam Bondi.

The White House and Blanche are under public pressure to show they are responding to questions about Epstein’s misconduct and the unreleased Epstein files.

President Donald Trump ran in 2024 vowing to bring those involved in illegal actions to justice, but last summer began dismissing the political controversy surrounding the files as a “hoax” conjured by political foes.

Blanche faced questions about his handling of the Epstein investigation during his Senate confirmation process. He told the committee there are “no closed investigations” in regard to Epstein’s crimes.

“If we learn today, if we learn next week, if we learn next month that there’s an individual we can investigate, indict and prosecute out of the Epstein files, you better believe that we will,” Blanche said at his confirmation hearing in July.

This summer, Comer told NOTUS he wanted to hold public hearings with some of Epstein’s victims, and signaled that he is working closely with victims as he moves to conclude the probe. It would be the first public hearing on the Epstein investigation.

Wrapping up the investigation means Comer must navigate the rocky internal politics inside his own party. Vice President JD Vance recently criticized the administration’s handling of the files in a podcast interview, a sentiment Comer echoed. But the congressman, like the vice president, has also downplayed Trump’s connection to Epstein, sharing the president’s argument that Democrats are engaged in a political witchhunt: “All [Democrats] care about on Epstein is Trump,” Comer told NOTUS.

Massie pointed to Vance’s comments as proof of the delicate balance some Republicans are trying to strike.

“[Vance is] at the same time trying to put daylight between himself and the debacle of the Epstein files that’s been committed by this administration, and also try to ameliorate the damage that’s been done there,” Massie told NOTUS.

For Democrats waiting in the wings to take over the investigation, there is a massive hole in the probe that they want to fill in.

“Quite frankly, there’s a lot of unanswered questions about the president,” Garcia said. “Until we get those 3 million documents released by the DOJ, this investigation is not going to be over.”
entries.author: Stephen Neukam

entries.title: Democrats’ Split on AI Grows as a New Plan Emerges
entries.summary: Senate Democrats’ top tax-writer proposes a tax on data centers.
entries.content:
Democrats looking for an alternative to progressive lawmakers’ proposed moratorium on data centers will now have yet another policy idea to consider.

Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, the highest-ranking Democrat on the Senate’s tax-writing body, on Thursday will propose a new excise tax and elimination of tax breaks for a data center construction boom expected to run into the trillions of dollars.

His proposal joins roughly a half-dozen competing Democratic approaches to addressing Americans’ unrest around AI, reflecting the soaring political salience of AI policy — an area Democrats are eager to win voters’ trust on.

“American communities are rightfully questioning whether the rapid build-out of data centers across the nation will benefit them, as local disruptions rise and Americans grow concerned about the long-term career prospects of millions of workers,” Wyden said. “These proposals are a first step towards safeguarding taxpayer dollars and ensuring there are resources to support American workers displaced by the coming disruptions to the economy.”

Wyden’s plan would prohibit data centers from benefiting from tax-advantaged “opportunity zones,” a tax deduction Republicans extended last year, and a tax incentive for real estate trusts. It would also level a new “low single-digit'” tax on company revenues. Data centers built in space would also be taxed if they provide services to U.S. customers.

Wyden doesn’t intend for the tax to stop the construction of data centers in the U.S. His office hasn’t determined where it would direct the new revenue from the tax. The surging stock market, driven largely by gains from AI, have minted many new billionaires and made Elon Musk the world’s first trillionaire.

Wyden’s proposal stands in stark contrast to that of Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York), who want to stop data center construction until guardrails can be put in place on artificial intelligence.

The party’s many differing policy proposals indicate AI could be an area of division within the party in the run-up to 2028.

Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas), chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, has pitched a tax on “tokens” that would charge AI companies per computing power used, rather than the revenue generated by data center operators. His idea would allow the federal revenue gained from the tax to scale with the rise in usage from AI. At least in theory, that would help ensure that the government has the funds to respond to potential layoffs, though some skeptics warn the costs could be passed on to consumers and businesses.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts) also teased her own plan in May in an op-ed in Time: a tax on the energy consumed by data centers that would also fall on the AI companies as well. Warren’s plan has been light on specifics but would likely raise substantial funds without shutting down the data centers. The proposal faces criticism from some who worry it would discourage the growth of the energy grid.

Meanwhile, Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California), who has said he is looking at running for president, has floated a “Data Center Bill of Rights” aimed at giving localities the legal authority to block data center projects if local investments aren’t made. Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Arizona), another possible presidential candidate, has proposed stripping tax breaks for data centers and for paying for upgrades they precipitate for local power grids.

While Wyden’s plan could raise billions from the AI companies, it’s a sharp departure from Sanders’ proposal to implement a 50 percent tax on the AI giants’ equity to bring them under government control. Sanders and Ocasio-Cortez have echoed warnings from AI safety experts that the technology poses existential threats to the U.S. economy and even humanity in calling for a complete moratorium on data center construction.

“AI and data centers are going to be a flash point for the next presidential election, and it’s good to see the chief tax writer in the Democratic Party take on this issue,” said Alex Jacquez, senior vice president at the Groundwork Collaborative, a left-leaning think tank, and a former Biden administration economic official. “It can’t be a substitute for all the other things we need to do. But the data centers need to be paying their fair share: These guys are getting fabulously wealthy, and it’s very clear the public is against them.”

So far, little has slowed the rapid advances in the technology powered by an estimated $130 billion increase in data center construction costs in the last year alone. Still, more than a dozen states have considered data center moratoriums of some kind, according to the Brookings Institution, a centrist think tank. Mitch Jones, deputy director of the advocacy group Food & Water Action, said new taxes alone would be "completely inadequate" to address the environmental and energy concerns primarily driving opposition to new data centers.

On the other hand, conservatives and industry groups have pushed back against the proposed restrictions and taxes. The data centers are essential to supporting the development of AI, and Republicans in particular have warned that slowing their growth could give China an enormous advantage in the race to develop the most powerful technology in world history.

But Democrats are looking at polling data that suggests the public is clamoring for federal action. Gallup polling in May found 7 in 10 Americans opposed construction of data centers near them. And the percentage of Americans who believe AI does “more harm than good” jumped from 31 percent last year to 39 percent this year, Gallup found in a separate poll.

“Democrats need a vision here. The technology is going to advance at a rapid scale, and we will be hit pretty quickly by a two-by-four and we have to do something,” said Rob Flaherty, a Democratic strategist who worked in the Biden White House. “On this issue, we have to figure out what we are for fast — capture this moment, or Republicans will do it for you.”
entries.author: Jeff Stein

entries.title: Wisconsin Democrats Doubt a Progressive’s Prospects After Michigan Results
entries.summary: Two gubernatorial candidates’ camps are drawing opposite conclusions after Abdul El-Sayed’s narrow victory on Tuesday
entries.content:
In Wisconsin, a progressive gubernatorial candidate is polling far ahead of the other candidates before the battleground state’s Democratic primary next week.

That was the story in Michigan, too: Polls showed Abdul El-Sayed handily beating Rep. Haley Stevens ahead of Tuesday’s Senate primary — but he had barely edged out a victory by the time the race was called the next morning. Now, some Democrats wonder if the same will come to pass in Wisconsin, where polling has shown state Rep. Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist, leading her opponents by double-digit margins for weeks.

Among the most doubtful is Hong’s leading opponent, David Crowley, who previously suspended his race in July because he wasn’t gaining traction before reentering 10 days later. Tuesday’s disconnect between polls and election day realities in Michigan brings Milwaukee County’s executive to one of the most optimistic points of his campaign so far. His team sent out an internal memo on Wednesday telling supporters his race is similarly closer than polls indicate.

“Results in Michigan Tuesday night showed polling that failed to appropriately capture and reflect the primary electorate and well overstated the position of the race frontrunner,” the memo, first reported by WISN, says. “Democrats are in the driver’s seat in Wisconsin to choose David Crowley and have the best fighting chance against Tom Tiffany in November.”

If next week’s voter base resembles those of 2018 and 2022, the primary “does not have a prohibitive front runner,” the memo continues.

While El-Sayed’s win shows how a socialist candidate like Hong can similarly ascend, Michigan’s uneven polling shows how challenging it is to pull off accurate primary surveys, said Barry Burden, a professor of political science at the University of Wisconsin-Madison — especially in Wisconsin and Michigan, where voters of any party can opt to participate.

“There are questions about where Hong stands,” Burden said. “There’s an opportunity for Crowley, and the Michigan results might be an indicator for him that it’s still a possibility.”

Wisconsin and Michigan are two of the country’s most consequential battleground states. Crowley’s camp argues Stevens’ better-than-expected performance proves more moderate candidates can still make good showings despite a recent progressive surge within the party.

“We don’t have to talk in theoreticals anymore about how this might work,” said a Democratic strategist who backs Crowley, given anonymity to candidly discuss the race. “Yeah, Haley didn't win, but she lost by one point. But this isn't us just trying to explain what our theory of the case is. … There is more money coming through the door today. There is more enthusiasm.”

Hong’s campaign, meanwhile, considers El-Sayed’s victory a harbinger of success in Wisconsin for the party’s left-most flank, which saw several candidates win Democratic primaries in New York City and Denver’s heavily blue districts. Michigan showed that working-class people are “ready for something different,” Hong said in a statement to NOTUS, adding that her campaign has “never taken the size of any projected margin for granted.”

“Polls are snapshots, and Michigan was another reminder that campaigns are won by organizing and turning out voters,” Hong said.

Stakes for Wisconsin Democrats are high in the state, which Trump won by less than a percentage point in 2024. The governor’s mansion, currently occupied by Democrat Tony Evers, has alternated between Republican and Democratic administrations since the 1970s. And the left’s gubernatorial candidate pool has ebbed and flowed significantly this summer — even prompting a lawsuit from the state party over the ability to recast ballots that was eventually dismissed.

Lt. Gov Sara Rodriguez dropped out of the race after reporting “serious mismanagement and inaccuracies” in her campaign finance filings. Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes ended his campaign last week shortly before the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reported it was looking into allegations of sexual impropriety. Crowley himself had dropped out of the race briefly before reentering with Evers’ endorsement.

Whoever advances from the Aug. 11 primary will face a tough race against Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany.

State Navigate, a polling firm that mostly focuses on state legislative races, concentrated on including more rural, low-income and Republican voters after seeing Michigan surveys miss those groups, executive director Chaz Nuttycombe said of a new survey coming out this week. A poll the organization conducted in late July showed Hong up by 29 points.

“It’ll probably be closer than people think based on the results in Michigan last night,” said another Democratic strategist in Wisconsin, granted anonymity to candidly discuss the race. “I think people thought that it was going to be a little more lopsided than it ended up being, and that’s probably what’s going to happen here in Wisconsin.”
entries.author: Christa Dutton

entries.title: Are Montana Democrats Abandoning Their Own Candidate?
entries.summary: Democratic leaders are backing an independent Senate candidate in Montana. The Democrat is livid.
entries.content:
Democrats are facing an unusual obstacle in their push to create as many paths to a Senate majority as possible this fall: a Democratic nominee who refuses to quit.

Democrat Alani Bankhead is set to face Republican Kurt Alme in Montana’s Senate election — the kind of race that would be a reach for Democrats in a normal year but could be on the table in a favorable political environment this year. The problem is Democrats are rallying behind independent candidate Seth Bodnar, who they think actually makes that long shot a possibility.

But with both candidates running, beating Alme is nearly impossible.

“[Republicans] know that if it’s head-to-head between Bodnar and Alme, Bodnar wins the damn race,” former Montana Sen. Jon Tester, who has endorsed Bodnar, told NOTUS.

Bankhead is livid with national party leadership, who she thinks is leaving her out to dry. In an interview with NOTUS, she accused Democratic leaders, nationally and in the state, of “using all their power and money to try to make Montanans accept the person that they pick.”

Bankhead alleges Tester has collaborated with the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer to circumvent the democratic process by backing a preferred candidate, an allegation Tester denies.

On top of that, it’s not even clear what would happen if Bankhead were to withdraw before next week’s Aug. 10 deadline. There’s a legal dispute, which lawyers briefed the state Democratic Party on, over whether the party would have to name a replacement for the party line should Bankhead quit. Bankhead has said repeatedly she is not considering exiting the race, “short of God” telling her to drop out.

“Montana law says no matter what — [even] if I die — the state party still has to replace me on the ballot,” Bankhead told NOTUS. “No, I’m not dropping out.”

In June, shortly after the Democratic primary, 17 state legislators wrote a letter to Bankhead and Bodnar, urging one of them to drop out.

“Every week that passes makes it more difficult to unify supporters, consolidate resources, and mount the strongest possible campaign for November,” the legislators wrote.

The lawmakers stopped short of supporting either candidate’s campaign.

“Based on the information currently available to us, Seth appears to have an advantage,” they wrote. “At the same time, we recognize that [Bankhead] has only recently secured the Democratic nomination.”

The state had at least one Democratic senator for a decade until 2024. But it’s not currently at the top of national Democrats’ priority list as they try to take the Senate majority in November.

“I’m just not tuned in on Montana,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts) told NOTUS. “I’ve been doing Michigan and Minnesota and Georgia and North Carolina.”

Several of her colleagues involved in other Senate races echoed that sentiment, including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont). But Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take the Senate majority, and some seats currently held by Democrats — including in Michigan — are in reach for Republicans, putting pressure on the party to devise multiple paths to victory.

Bankhead, a retired Air Force lieutenant colonel and counterintelligence agent who won the state's Democratic primary with over 48,000 votes in June, faces myriad challenges.

Bankhead’s campaign had only raised just under $60,000 by the end of June compared to the more than $3.2 million Bodnar has raised since launching his campaign. Bankhead accuses the DSCC of “starving” her campaign of money — and she is facing mounting pressurefrom former Democratic leaders in the state to drop out.

A Tavern Research poll conducted in mid-June, showed an Alme-Bodnar tie in a hypothetical head-to-head, while Alme led Bankhead 56-44 in a hypothetical two-way race. Some polls show Bodnar leading Alme if Bankhead were to drop out.

There has been a run of Democratic Senate nominees withdrawing to clear the path for a two-way race with an independent candidate. Democratic nominees have dropped their campaigns in Nebraska, South Dakota and Idaho, giving a boost to independent candidates in each Republican-leaning state.

Bodnar, the former president of the University of Montana and a West Point-trained former Green Beret, entered the race as an independent in late March. He has secured the endorsement of major Democratic-aligned groups, including Montana Conservation Voters and VoteVets — the largest progressive veterans’ organization in the U.S. The group previously supported Bankhead.

Bodnar also has been endorsed by Tester and former Democratic Sen. Max Baucus, among other leaders.

Bodnar’s campaign did not respond to NOTUS’ request for comment.

Bankhead described herself as being up against the entrenched party establishment.

“Old guard political leaders want to stay in power and control, and they're trying to use the last bit of power that they have to wield their influence to maintain the status quo,” she told NOTUS.

Schumer’s office did not respond to NOTUS’ request for comment.

The DSCC referred NOTUS to theorganization’s comments to Semafor, where DSCC executive director Devan Barber said “The DSCC partners with viable campaigns who have a path to victory, which Ms. Bankhead does not.”

Montana’s Senate seat is open because Republican Sen. Steve Daines abruptly withdrew in March and endorsed Alme, who had filed to run the same day. Concerns over splitting the Democratic vote have local leaders convinced that keeping Bankhead on the ballot will hand Republicans an easy win in the state.

Bodnar, Tester said in the interview, is “the kind of person who’s willing to sit down and listen, and make a decision based on facts, not on conspiracy theories. And for that reason, he’s head and shoulders above the people who he’s running against.”

Tester also says Bodnar’s candidacy is viable not because he is an independent, but because “he is somebody that understands politics,” working families, high costs, agriculture and the “shit that this president with support of the Congress have done.”

While most Senate Democrats NOTUS spoke to repeatedly said they had not been paying close attention to the Montana race, some said they were relying on Tester to know the best path to contention in the state.

“I have a lot of respect for Tester, and so I kind of defer to him in terms of just what can be done,” Sen. Andy Kim of New Jersey told NOTUS.
entries.author: Raymond Fernández
